Avoid C-style variadic functions in C++
WHAT: Defining or using C-style variadic functions (with `...`) allows callers to pass arguments with unchecked types or counts, causing undefined behavior when arguments are missing or of the wrong type.
WHY: Undefined behavior in variadic calls can corrupt memory or control flow and may be exploitable to execute arbitrary code.
HOW: Do not define C-style variadic functions; instead, use C++ variadic templates (parameter packs), overloading, or currying to handle variable arguments safely.
EXAMPLE (C++): Before: `int sum(int first, ...);` and using `va_list` internally. After: `template<typename... Args> int sum(Args... args);` using type-safe parameter packs.
Avoid C-style variadic functions in C++
WHAT: Using C-style variadic functions (e.g., with `...`, `va_list`, `va_start`, `va_arg`, `va_end`) can cause undefined behavior when arguments are not correctly terminated or types do not match the expected format.
WHY: Undefined behavior can lead to memory corruption, crashes, or exploitable conditions due to reading incorrect types or out-of-bounds stack data.
HOW: Replace C-style variadic functions with type-safe C++ alternatives such as variadic templates and parameter packs, and constrain argument types using mechanisms like `std::enable_if` and type traits.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `int add(int first, int second, ...);` using `va_list` logic. After (safer): `template<typename Arg, typename... Ts> int add(Arg f, Ts... rest) { static_assert(std::is_integral<Arg>::value, "integral only"); return f + add(rest...); }`.

WHAT: Defining C-style variadic functions (using `...` and `va_list`) in C++ leads to loss of type safety and unsafe argument handling.
WHY: Mismatched types or counts of arguments cannot be checked by the compiler, which can cause memory corruption, crashes, or logic errors.
HOW: Use C++ variadic templates and braced initializer lists to expand parameter packs, relying on compile-time type traits (`std::enable_if`, `std::is_integral`, etc.) to enforce type constraints; only use C-style variadics when required for C linkage APIs.
EXAMPLE (C++): Before: `int sum(const char *fmt, ...);` using `va_list` internally. After: `template<typename... Ts> int sum(Ts... args) { int values[] = { args... }; /* iterate safely */ }` using a braced initializer list to preserve type safety.
Do not define C-style variadic function templates
WHAT: Using C-style variadic function templates (e.g., `template <typename> static T test(...);`) can cause unintended overload resolution and hide type errors, especially when combined with SFINAE and unevaluated contexts.
WHY: Mis-resolved overloads may bypass intended checks, leading to incorrect behavior, logic flaws, or use of unintended code paths that can undermine security assumptions.
HOW: Avoid C-style variadic function templates; instead, use safer alternatives such as function overloading with fixed parameter types, parameter packs (`template <typename... Args>`), or explicit trait/enable_if constructs that do not rely on `...`.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe pattern): `template <typename> static no& test(...);` → After (safer): use `template <typename U, typename = decltype(std::declval<U>().foo())> static yes& test(U*);` and omit any `...`-based overload.
Do not declare or define reserved identifiers in C++
WHAT: Declaring, defining, or macro-defining identifiers that are reserved by the C++ implementation (for example, names with double underscores, leading underscore+capital, standard library names, or keywords/attributes) causes undefined behavior.
WHY: Undefined behavior can lead to subtle security vulnerabilities, including corrupted control flow, broken library invariants, and exploitable crashes that vary across compilers and platforms.
HOW: Avoid using any identifier that is reserved: do not #define/#undef standard library names or keywords/attributes; do not use names with “__”, leading “_” followed by uppercase, or leading “_” in the global namespace; do not reuse standard library object, function, or type names with external linkage.
EXAMPLE: Before (noncompliant, C++): `#define std printf` or `int __secret;` or `int _File;`
After (compliant): use application-specific names without leading underscores or double underscores, and never redefine standard or keyword names, for example `int app_secret;`

WHAT: Using reserved identifiers (for example, header guards with leading/trailing underscores or user-defined literal suffixes without required underscores) can clash with implementation- or library-reserved names.
WHY: Name collisions with compiler or standard library internals can cause undefined behavior, compilation errors, or subtle miscompilations.

WHAT: Declaring or defining identifiers that begin with an underscore at file scope (for variables, functions, literals, etc.) can clash with implementation-reserved names, causing undefined behavior or linkage conflicts.

Avoid cv-qualifying C++ reference types
WHAT: Declaring references with const or volatile qualifiers (for example, `char &const p`) instead of qualifying the referenced type (for example, `const char &p`) is ill-formed and can lead to undefined behavior if not diagnosed.
WHY: Misqualified references may compile on nonconforming compilers and allow unintended mutation of data that is assumed to be immutable, breaking invariants and causing unpredictable behavior.
HOW: Never apply const/volatile directly to a reference type; always qualify the underlying pointee type instead. Use `const T&` or `T const&` for read-only references, and configure builds to treat such diagnostics as errors.
EXAMPLE: Before (incorrect): `void f(char c) { char &const p = c; p = 'p'; }`
EXAMPLE: After (correct): `void f(const char &c) { /* c cannot be modified */ }`

WHAT: Using const (or volatile) on a reference type (e.g., const char& p) can create ill-formed or misleading code where a supposedly read-only reference is modified, with behavior differing across compilers.
WHY: Such inconsistencies can lead to compilation errors or subtle logic bugs that may undermine assumptions about immutability and program correctness.
HOW: Do not apply const or volatile directly to reference types; instead, qualify the referenced type appropriately and ensure code does not attempt to assign through a reference to const data.
EXAMPLE: Noncompliant: `void f(char c){ const char &p = c; p = 'p'; }` → Compliant: `void f(char c){ char &p = c; p = 'p'; }`
Avoid syntactically ambiguous C++ declarations
WHAT: Ambiguous C++ syntax that can be parsed either as a declaration or as an expression (for example, function-style casts vs. function declarations) can cause the compiler to interpret code differently than intended.
WHY: Misparsed declarations can change program behavior, hide logic errors, and lead to subtle, hard-to-detect bugs that may undermine security assumptions.
HOW: Use uniform initialization with braced-init-lists for object initialization, avoid function-style casts in declarations, prefer `=` initialization, and remove redundant parentheses around parameter names so that declarations are unambiguous.
EXAMPLE: Before (ambiguous): `Widget w(OtherType());`
After (clear declaration): `Widget w{OtherType{}};` or `Widget w = OtherType();`
Avoid syntactically ambiguous RAII lock declarations
WHAT: Ambiguous declarations like `std::unique_lock<std::mutex>(m);` can be parsed as a temporary object instead of a named lock, leaving the mutex unlocked while accessing shared data.
WHY: Failing to actually acquire the mutex before using shared resources can cause race conditions, data corruption, and security vulnerabilities in concurrent code.
HOW: Always declare RAII lock objects with a clear identifier and constructor call (e.g., `std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(m);`), and avoid declaration forms that can be parsed as temporary objects or function declarations.
EXAMPLE (C++): Before: `std::unique_lock<std::mutex>(m); shared_resource += 42;` After: `std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(m); shared_resource += 42;`
Avoid syntactically ambiguous C++ declarations
WHAT: Ambiguous C++ declarations (e.g., `Widget w();` inside a function) can be parsed as function declarations instead of variable definitions, so constructors or initialization code never execute as intended.
WHY: Missing initialization can silently skip security-critical setup (e.g., zeroization, capability checks, invariant enforcement), leading to undefined behavior or bypassed protections.
HOW: When declaring local objects, avoid declaration forms that can be parsed as functions: elide empty parentheses (`Widget w;`) or use brace initialization (`Widget w{};`) to force object construction.
EXAMPLE: Noncompliant: `void f() { Widget w(); }`
EXAMPLE: Compliant: `void f() { Widget w; Widget w2{}; }`

WHAT: Ambiguous C++ declarations (for example, `Gadget g(Widget(i));`) can be parsed as function declarations instead of object constructions, so expected constructors are never called.
WHY: Skipped construction or initialization can leave objects uninitialized or logic unexecuted, leading to undefined behavior, logic flaws, or security vulnerabilities.
HOW: Avoid declaration forms that can be parsed as functions; prefer uniform initialization (`Gadget g{Widget{i}};`), factory functions, or clearly separate declarations from calls; enable compiler warnings that detect vexing parses and fix all occurrences.
EXAMPLE: Before (ambiguous): `Gadget g(Widget(i));`
After (unambiguous): `Gadget g{Widget{i}};`
Avoid syntactically ambiguous C++ declarations
WHAT: Ambiguous C++ declarations (e.g., that can be parsed as either a variable or a function declaration) can cause the compiler to create a different entity than intended, leading to logic errors.
WHY: Mis-declared objects may never be constructed or used as expected, breaking control flow, resource management, or security checks that rely on those objects.

Overload allocation and deallocation functions as a pair in the same scope
WHAT: Overloading operator new (or other allocation function) without overloading the corresponding operator delete (or deallocation function) in the same scope can cause objects to be freed with an incompatible deallocator, leading to undefined behavior.
WHY: Mismatched allocation/deallocation can corrupt heaps, leak memory, or crash the program, especially when using custom/private heaps or allocators.
HOW: Whenever you overload an allocation function (global or class-scope), also overload the matching deallocation function in the same scope; only omit the pair when the function is explicitly deleted or declared private and left undefined to prevent use.
EXAMPLE: Before (noncompliant, C++): `void* operator new(std::size_t s){ return custom_alloc(s); } // no matching operator delete`. After (compliant): `void* operator new(std::size_t s){ return custom_alloc(s); } void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { custom_free(p); }`.
Overload allocation and deallocation functions as a matched pair in the same scope
WHAT: Defining a custom allocation function (e.g., operator new or a heap alloc wrapper) without a corresponding deallocation function in the same scope can cause mismatched memory management and leaks.
WHY: Mismatched or missing deallocation leads to memory leaks, undefined behavior, and potential denial-of-service from resource exhaustion.
HOW: Whenever you overload or wrap an allocation function, also define and expose the matching deallocation function in the same scope and ensure all allocations are freed via that pair.
EXAMPLE: In C++, if you define a global `void* operator new(std::size_t)` using a custom heap, also define a global `void operator delete(void*)` that frees memory from the same heap.
Overload allocation and deallocation operators as a matched pair in the same scope
WHAT: Overloading operator new without overloading the corresponding operator delete in the same class or scope leaves objects in an indeterminate state when deleted, breaking allocation bookkeeping.
WHY: Mismatched allocation/deallocation can corrupt memory, leak resources, or cause undefined behavior that attackers may exploit for memory-safety vulnerabilities.
HOW: Whenever you overload operator new (or other allocation functions) for a class or scope, also overload the corresponding operator delete (and sized variants where applicable) in the same scope, ensuring both consistently update any bookkeeping.
EXAMPLE (C++ – before): struct S { void *operator new(std::size_t s) { void *p = ::operator new(s); update_bookkeeping(p,s,true); return p; } };
EXAMPLE (C++ – after): struct S { void *operator new(std::size_t s){ void *p=::operator new(s); update_bookkeeping(p,s,true); return p;} void operator delete(void *p,std::size_t s) noexcept { ::operator delete(p); update_bookkeeping(p,s,false);} };
Overload allocation and deallocation functions as a pair in the same scope
WHAT: Failing to provide a matching deallocation function for an overloaded allocation function in the same scope can cause memory to never be freed when exceptions occur during object construction.
WHY: Missing or mismatched deallocation leads to memory leaks and potential resource exhaustion, especially when exceptions terminate initialization.
HOW: Whenever you overload an allocation function (including placement new), define the corresponding deallocation function in the same scope, unless object construction is guaranteed noexcept(true) and exceptions are globally disabled.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `void* operator new(std::size_t sz, MyTag);` // no matching delete. After (safe): `void* operator new(std::size_t sz, MyTag); void operator delete(void* p, MyTag) noexcept;`
Avoid information leakage in class object padding across trust boundaries
WHAT: Passing a C++ class object (or pointer/reference to it) across a trust boundary can leak sensitive data via uninitialized padding bits inside the object.
WHY: Padding bits may contain indeterminate values from prior memory usage, exposing secrets (keys, passwords, internal state) to less-trusted code or remote parties.
HOW: Before sending or sharing a class object across a trust boundary, ensure all padding is deterministically initialized (for example, zero-initialize the whole storage, then assign fields) or serialize only explicit fields into a separate, fully initialized transfer structure.
EXAMPLE: Before: `MyMsg msg; msg.id = userId; send(&msg, sizeof(msg));` After: `MyMsg msg{}; msg.id = userId; send(&msg, sizeof(msg));` or serialize only `id` into a packed transfer buffer.

WHAT: Copying whole C++ objects (e.g., with `sizeof(obj)`) across a trust boundary can leak uninitialized padding bytes that may contain sensitive kernel or process data.
WHY: Attackers receiving these leaked bytes can infer internal state, bypass protections, or exfiltrate confidential information.
HOW: Never copy raw class/struct objects across trust boundaries; instead, define an explicit serialized representation and copy only fully initialized, non-padded fields (e.g., pack into a POD buffer or use a serialization routine).

Before: `copy_to_user(usr_buf, &arg, sizeof(arg));`
After:  `struct { int a; int c; char b; } safe{}; safe.a=arg.a; safe.c=arg.c; safe.b=arg.b; copy_to_user(usr_buf, &safe, sizeof(safe));`

WHAT: Copying a C++ object’s raw memory (including padding bytes) to a less-trusted context (e.g., user space) can leak uninitialized or stale register data via padding bytes.
WHY: Leaked padding bytes may contain sensitive information from previous computations, leading to unintended data disclosure.
HOW: Do not use raw memory copies (e.g., memcpy, copy_to_user with sizeof(object)) on non-trivially copyable objects; instead, copy only explicitly initialized fields into a dedicated POD/struct with no padding or serialize fields individually.

WHAT: Copying raw class/struct objects (for example, via memcpy of the whole object) across a trust boundary can leak uninitialized padding bytes to untrusted code.
WHY: Leaked padding may contain sensitive data from prior stack/heap usage, leading to information disclosure vulnerabilities.
HOW: Do not copy entire objects blindly; instead, explicitly serialize only initialized fields into a packed buffer and send only the exact number of bytes written. On the receiving side, reconstruct the object from the serialized fields.

WHY: Attackers may read sensitive data from uninitialized padding bytes, leading to information disclosure.

WHAT: Failing to fully initialize all fields (including padding and reserved fields) of objects or structs before copying them across a trust boundary can leak uninitialized memory contents.
WHY: Attackers can read sensitive kernel or process memory, potentially exposing secrets, internal state, or enabling further exploitation.

Avoid cycles during initialization of static objects
WHAT: Static or thread-local variables whose initialization reenters the defining function or depends on other statics with undefined order can cause recursive initialization, deadlock, or undefined behavior.
WHY: Undefined behavior and deadlocks can lead to crashes, denial of service, or unpredictable program state that may be exploitable.
HOW: Ensure static initialization code does not call back into the same function or into code that depends on other not-yet-initialized statics; break dependency cycles, use lazy initialization with explicit guards, or replace statics with objects whose lifetime is explicitly controlled.
EXAMPLE: Before (problematic): `int f() { static X x = X(f()); return 0; }` — `f()` is reentered during `x`’s initialization. After (fixed): `int f() { static X x; static bool inited = false; if (!inited) { x.init_without_calling_f(); inited = true; } return 0; }`
Avoid cycles during initialization of static objects
WHAT: Creating initialization interdependencies or recursion among static objects with dynamic initialization (especially across translation units) causes unordered or cyclic initialization and can lead to deadlock or undefined behavior.
WHY: Unspecified or undefined initialization order can cause deadlocks in thread-safe initialization, crashes, or incorrect program state, which may be exploitable in security-sensitive code.
HOW: Do not call functions that depend (directly or indirectly) on the same static object from its initializer; avoid recursion in static initializers; prefer constexpr or simple literal initialization, and refactor complex initialization into explicit startup routines called in a well-defined order.
EXAMPLE: Before (noncompliant): `static const int cache[] = { fact(0), fact(1), ... };` where `fact()` uses `cache`. After (compliant): initialize `cache` with fixed constants or fill it in a separate initialization function called before `fact()` is used.
Avoid cycles during initialization of static objects
WHAT: Static objects that depend on each other during initialization can cause undefined behavior, crashes, or incorrect values due to cyclic initialization order.
WHY: Cyclic initialization may execute code on partially initialized objects, leading to logic errors, security vulnerabilities, or denial of service.
HOW: Use lazy initialization with zero-initialized static storage; defer complex initialization until first use, and ensure recursive calls do not trigger re-entrant initialization of the same static object.
EXAMPLE: Before: `static Obj a = Obj(b); static Obj b = Obj(a);` After: `Obj& a(){ static Obj a_inst = Obj(b()); return a_inst; } Obj& b(){ static Obj b_inst = Obj(a()); return b_inst; }`
Avoid static initialization order dependencies in C++ global objects
WHAT: Static or global objects in different translation units depend on each other’s constructors (for example, one’s initializer calls methods on another), causing unspecified initialization order and unpredictable values.
WHY: Unspecified initialization order can lead to logic errors, inconsistent configuration, or latent vulnerabilities when security-critical state or configuration is initialized incorrectly.
HOW: Eliminate cross-TU initialization dependencies by using function-local statics (“construct on first use”), avoiding global objects whose initializers call into other globals, or replacing such globals with initialization functions explicitly invoked from main() in a defined order.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `extern Car c; int numWheels = c.get_num_wheels();` in one file and `Car c = get_default_car();` in another; After (safer): `int numWheels() { static Car c = get_default_car(); return c.get_num_wheels(); }` and call `numWheels()` from main() or other functions.
Avoid static initialization order cycles in C++ global/static objects
WHAT: Static or global objects that depend on each other across translation units can create initialization order cycles, causing reads of uninitialized data or undefined behavior.
WHY: Incorrect initialization order can lead to subtle, intermittent bugs, crashes, or security vulnerabilities due to use of partially constructed objects.
HOW: Use the “construct on first use” idiom: move dependent static objects into function-local static variables so they are initialized on first use, after all required globals are safely initialized.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `static int numWheels = c.get_num_wheels();` where `c` is a global in another file. After (safer): `int &get_num_wheels() { extern Car c; static int numWheels = c.get_num_wheels(); return numWheels; }`
Avoid cycles during initialization of static objects
WHAT: Static or class-level objects that depend on each other during initialization can create initialization cycles, leading to undefined order, use of uninitialized data, or deadlock.
WHY: Initialization cycles can cause crashes, corrupted state, or unpredictable behavior that may be exploitable in security-sensitive code paths.

Do not let exceptions escape from destructors or deallocation functions
WHAT: Throwing exceptions from C++ destructors or deallocation functions (operator delete/delete[]) causes undefined behavior or calls std::terminate/std::abort, leaving objects undestroyed and program state indeterminate.
WHY: Escaping exceptions during destruction or deallocation can bypass cleanup, corrupt program state, and lead to crashes or security vulnerabilities due to inconsistent resource release.
HOW: Ensure destructors and deallocation functions are noexcept (implicitly or explicitly), catch all internal exceptions, handle or log them locally, and never declare these functions noexcept(false) or allow them to propagate exceptions.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `~Obj() { may_throw(); }`
After (safe): `~Obj() noexcept { try { may_throw(); } catch (...) { log_error(); /* no rethrow */ } }`
Avoid exceptions escaping from C++ destructors or deallocation functions
WHAT: Throwing exceptions from destructors or deallocation functions (especially during stack unwinding) can cause undefined behavior or terminate the program, and workarounds like std::uncaught_exception() may skip critical cleanup.
WHY: Unexpected termination or skipped destructor logic can leak resources, leave data in inconsistent states, or break security assumptions about cleanup and rollback.
HOW: Design destructors and deallocation functions to be noexcept and never throw; handle all errors internally (logging, setting error flags, or using non-throwing error channels) and ensure all resources are released regardless of error conditions.
EXAMPLE (C++): Before: `~S() noexcept(false) { if (has_error()) throw std::logic_error("bad"); }` After: `~S() noexcept { if (has_error()) log_error(); /* always release resources */ }`
Do not let exceptions escape from destructors or deallocation functions
WHAT: Destructors or deallocation functions that allow exceptions to propagate (including via implicit rethrow from a function-try-block handler) can terminate the program during stack unwinding.
WHY: Unhandled exceptions during destruction can cause abnormal termination, resource leaks, and leave data in an inconsistent or partially destroyed state.
HOW: Ensure destructors only call non-throwing operations, or catch all exceptions and prevent control from reaching the end of the handler (for example, by handling and then returning), so no exception can escape.
EXAMPLE (C++):
Before: `~SomeClass() try { /* use Bad */ } catch (...) { /* log */ }`
After:  `~SomeClass() noexcept { try { /* use Bad */ } catch (...) { /* log, cleanup */ return; } }`
Avoid exceptions from C++ destructors and deallocation functions
WHAT: Throwing exceptions from destructors or global deallocation functions (e.g., operator delete) causes undefined behavior or program termination when another exception is active.
WHY: Exceptions escaping these functions can lead to double-fault termination, resource leaks, memory corruption, or inconsistent program state.
HOW: Mark destructors and deallocation functions as noexcept (or leave default noexcept for delete), catch all internal exceptions, handle/log them locally, and ensure control flow does not rethrow (e.g., use explicit return in function-try-block).
EXAMPLE:
// Before: void operator delete(void* p) noexcept(false) { if (perform_dealloc(p)) throw std::logic_error("bad"); }
// After:  void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (perform_dealloc(p)) { /* log/abort/cleanup, but do not throw */ } }

WHY: Using a NULL or invalid pointer can cause crashes or enable exploits that write to unintended memory locations, compromising integrity and control flow.
HOW: After every dynamic allocation (malloc/calloc/realloc/new), immediately check for failure (NULL or exception) and abort, clean up, or safely degrade before any dereference or pointer arithmetic.
EXAMPLE (C++): Before: `int *p = (int*)calloc(n, sizeof(int)); p[0] = 1;` After: `int *p = (int*)calloc(n, sizeof(int)); if (!p) { handle_error(); return; } p[0] = 1;`
Explicit object construction and destruction in manual lifetime management
WHAT: Failing to explicitly call constructors and destructors when manually managing C++ object lifetimes (e.g., memory from malloc or custom allocators) leads to using objects that were never initialized or never finalized.
WHY: Using objects outside their lifetime causes undefined behavior, including data corruption, crashes, and security vulnerabilities from reading/writing invalid or uninitialized memory.
HOW: When you obtain raw storage without new (malloc, custom allocator, slabs), start the object’s lifetime with placement new (or equivalent explicit construction) and end it by explicitly invoking the destructor before releasing or reusing the storage.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `void* p = malloc(sizeof(T)); T* t = (T*)p; /* use *t */ free(p);` After (safe): `void* p = malloc(sizeof(T)); T* t = new(p) T(/*args*/); /* use *t */ t->~T(); free(p);`
Explicit object construction and destruction when manually managing C++ object lifetime
WHAT: Failing to call constructors/destructors when using raw memory (e.g., std::malloc/std::free) for objects with nontrivial initialization causes undefined behavior when the object is accessed.
WHY: Undefined behavior can lead to memory corruption, crashes, or exploitable security vulnerabilities due to use of improperly initialized or destroyed objects.
HOW: When using manual allocation for such objects, allocate raw storage, then explicitly construct with placement new and explicitly call the destructor before freeing the storage; keep raw storage and live-object pointers separate to avoid use outside lifetime.
EXAMPLE:
Before: S *s = static_cast<S *>(std::malloc(sizeof(S))); s->f(); std::free(s);
After: void *ptr = std::malloc(sizeof(S)); S *s = new (ptr) S; s->f(); s->~S(); std::free(ptr);
Explicitly construct and destruct objects when manually managing object lifetime
WHAT: Manually allocated storage for objects (for example, via allocators or raw memory) is used without explicitly invoking constructors for all elements, leading to access of uninitialized or non-constructed objects through operators like operator[]().
WHY: Accessing objects whose constructors were never run causes undefined behavior, which can lead to memory corruption, data leaks, or exploitable crashes.
HOW: After allocating raw storage, explicitly construct every element (e.g., via placement new or allocator::construct) before any read/write access, and explicitly destroy all constructed elements (e.g., allocator::destroy) before deallocation; ensure reserve/resize-like functions both allocate and construct new elements.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `T *p = alloc.allocate(count); copy_elements(old, p, numElements);` then `numElements = count;` and `operator[](i)` may access unconstructed `p[i]`. After (safe): after allocation and copying, loop from `numElements` to `count` and call `std::allocator_traits<Alloc>::construct(alloc, &p[i]);` to default-construct remaining elements before updating `numElements` and exposing them.
Explicit object construction and destruction in manual lifetime management
WHAT: Failing to explicitly construct and destruct non-trivially constructible/destructible objects when manually managing storage (e.g., via allocators or raw memory) can leave objects uninitialized or improperly destroyed.
WHY: This can cause undefined behavior, including memory corruption, use of uninitialized data, and resource leaks.
HOW: When using manual allocation (e.g., allocator::allocate, operator new, raw buffers), explicitly invoke constructors (e.g., allocator::construct or placement new) for each non-trivial object and ensure corresponding destruction (e.g., allocator::destroy) before deallocation; skip explicit calls only for types verified as trivially constructible/destructible via std::is_trivially_constructible / std::is_trivially_destructible.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): T* p = alloc.allocate(count); /* use p[i] without constructing */ … alloc.deallocate(p, count); After (safe): T* p = alloc.allocate(count); for (size_t i=0;i<count;++i) alloc.construct(&p[i]); /* use p[i] */ for (size_t i=0;i<count;++i) alloc.destroy(&p[i]); alloc.deallocate(p, count);
Explicit construction and destruction for manual object lifetime
WHAT: Failing to explicitly construct or destruct objects when manually managing lifetime (e.g., via placement new or custom allocators) can leave objects uninitialized, partially constructed, or never destroyed.
WHY: This can cause use of invalid object state, memory corruption, resource leaks, and undefined behavior exploitable for security vulnerabilities.
HOW: When using raw storage or custom allocation, always invoke constructors with placement new and explicitly call destructors before releasing the underlying storage; avoid mixing manual lifetime control with automatic storage management.
EXAMPLE: (C++) Before: `void* p = ::operator new(sizeof(T)); T* t = (T*)p; /* use t */ ::operator delete(p);` After: `void* p = ::operator new(sizeof(T)); T* t = new (p) T(); /* use t */ t->~T(); ::operator delete(p);`
Placement new alignment and capacity
WHAT: Misusing placement new by passing a pointer that is misaligned or does not reference sufficient storage for the target object/array, causing construction at an invalid location or writing past the buffer.
WHY: This leads to undefined behavior, including memory corruption, out-of-bounds writes, and potential security vulnerabilities such as crashes or code execution.
HOW: Before calling placement new, ensure the pointer is aligned for the target type (e.g., via std::aligned_storage or aligned allocation APIs) and that the underlying buffer is at least sizeof(T) (or sizeof(T) * count plus any required overhead for arrays); never reuse arbitrary or undersized buffers.
EXAMPLE: Before: `char buf[sizeof(T)]; T* p = new (buf) T();` (may be misaligned). After: `std::aligned_storage_t<sizeof(T), alignof(T)> buf; T* p = new (&buf) T();`
Provide placement new with properly aligned pointers to sufficient storage capacity
WHAT: Using placement new with a pointer to an object that is too small or improperly aligned for the target type (for example, constructing a long in storage for a short) causes undefined behavior.
WHY: Undefined behavior can lead to memory corruption, crashes, or exploitable vulnerabilities due to overwritten or misaligned data.
HOW: Ensure the storage passed to placement new is at least sizeof(T) bytes and correctly aligned for T; typically allocate storage as an array of std::byte/unsigned char sized to sizeof(T) and aligned using alignas(T) or std::aligned_storage/std::aligned_alloc.
EXAMPLE:
Before (noncompliant): short s; long *lp = ::new (&s) long;
After (compliant): alignas(long) unsigned char buf[sizeof(long)]; long *lp = ::new (buf) long;
Placement new must use properly aligned storage
WHAT: Using placement new with a pointer to storage that is not correctly aligned for the target type (for example, a raw char buffer) can cause undefined behavior when constructing the object.
WHY: Misaligned accesses can lead to crashes, data corruption, or exploitable undefined behavior on architectures that require strict alignment.
HOW: When using placement new, ensure the target buffer is both large enough and aligned for the constructed type, for example by declaring it with alignas(T) or using std::aligned_storage with sizeof(T) and alignof(T).
EXAMPLE: Before (noncompliant, misaligned buffer): `unsigned char buffer[sizeof(long)]; long* lp = ::new (buffer) long;` After (compliant, aligned buffer): `alignas(long) unsigned char buffer[sizeof(long)]; long* lp = ::new (buffer) long;`
Placement new with insufficient storage for array overhead
WHAT: Failing to account for implementation-specific array overhead (“cookie”) when using placement new for arrays can result in writing past the end of the provided buffer.
WHY: Overwriting adjacent memory can corrupt data, cause crashes, or enable memory-safety vulnerabilities such as arbitrary code execution.
HOW: When using placement new for arrays, allocate storage that is at least the size required by the implementation for the array (including any overhead), or avoid placement new for arrays and instead use standard allocation mechanisms (e.g., new[], containers) that handle overhead correctly.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `alignas(S) unsigned char buf[sizeof(S)*N]; S* sp = ::new (buf) S[N];` After (safer): use `std::vector<S> v(N);` or a standard `S* sp = new S[N];` so the implementation manages any array overhead.
Provide placement new with properly aligned pointers to sufficient storage capacity
WHAT: When using placement new[] with a user-supplied buffer, failing to account for implementation-specific array-new overhead and element size can cause buffer overflows or misaligned object storage.
WHY: Mis-sized or misaligned buffers lead to memory corruption, undefined behavior, and potential security vulnerabilities such as data corruption or code execution.
HOW: Determine the allocator’s array-new overhead for the target compiler, ensure the buffer is properly aligned for the object type, and verify at runtime that the buffer size is at least sizeof(T) * count + overhead before constructing the array.
EXAMPLE (C++): Before: `alignas(S) unsigned char buf[sizeof(S)*n]; S* p = new (buf) S[n];` After: `const size_t overhead = sizeof(size_t); alignas(S) unsigned char buf[sizeof(S)*n + overhead]; if (sizeof(buf) < sizeof(S)*n + overhead) throw std::bad_array_new_length(); S* p = new (buf, sizeof(buf)) S[n];`
Provide placement new with properly aligned pointers to sufficient storage capacity
WHAT: Using placement new with pointers that are misaligned or refer to insufficient storage can cause undefined behavior, including memory corruption.
WHY: Misaligned or undersized storage can lead to crashes, data corruption, or exploitable memory safety vulnerabilities.
HOW: Ensure the target storage is at least sizeof(T) bytes and aligned to alignof(T); use std::aligned_storage or properly aligned buffers, and never reuse smaller or incorrectly aligned memory for larger types.
EXAMPLE:
Before: `char buf[4]; T* p = new (buf) T;`
After: `std::aligned_storage_t<sizeof(T), alignof(T)> buf; T* p = new (&buf) T;`
Honor replacement dynamic storage management requirements
WHAT: Custom replacements for dynamic memory allocation/deallocation functions that do not fully implement the required standard semantics cause undefined behavior.
WHY: Undefined behavior can lead to memory corruption, crashes, data leaks, or exploitable vulnerabilities in any code using the allocator.
HOW: When replacing global new/delete (and related allocation APIs), strictly implement all required behaviors from the C++ Standard, including error handling, alignment, size semantics, and interaction with standard library components.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): custom operator new ignores requested size and never throws or returns nullptr as required; After (safe): custom operator new respects the size parameter, alignment, failure behavior, and other semantic requirements defined for operator new.
Honor replacement dynamic storage management requirements
WHAT: Custom replacements for global operator new(std::size_t) that return nullptr on allocation failure instead of throwing std::bad_alloc violate the required behavior and can cause callers to dereference null pointers.
WHY: Code that assumes operator new throws on failure may skip null checks, leading to null pointer dereferences, crashes, or undefined behavior.
HOW: When replacing global operator new, strictly match the C++ Standard requirements: on allocation failure, throw std::bad_alloc (or call the new_handler and then throw) instead of returning nullptr; ensure paired operator delete overloads are correctly declared.
EXAMPLE:
Before (noncompliant): void* operator new(std::size_t size) { extern void* alloc_mem(std::size_t); return alloc_mem(size); }
After (compliant): void* operator new(std::size_t size) { if (void* p = alloc_mem(size)) return p; throw std::bad_alloc(); }
Avoid unrelated smart pointers owning the same raw pointer
WHAT: Creating a new smart pointer (or calling reset()) with a raw pointer already owned by another smart pointer causes multiple unrelated owners of the same object, leading to double delete or use-after-free.
WHY: Double deletion or dangling pointers can result in memory corruption, crashes, or exploitable vulnerabilities.
HOW: Only create additional smart pointers by copying or moving existing smart pointers; never construct or reset a smart pointer directly from a raw pointer that is already managed by another smart pointer.
EXAMPLE (C++ before): `std::unique_ptr<int> a(new int(1)); std::shared_ptr<int> b(a.get());`
EXAMPLE (C++ after): `std::shared_ptr<int> a = std::make_shared<int>(1); std::shared_ptr<int> b = a;`
Do not store an already-owned pointer value in an unrelated smart pointer
WHAT: Creating multiple unrelated smart pointers (for example, separate std::shared_ptr instances) from the same raw pointer causes each to believe it uniquely owns the object, leading to double-free and use-after-free when they are destroyed.
WHY: Double-free and use-after-free can cause memory corruption, crashes, or arbitrary code execution.
HOW: Never construct a new smart pointer directly from a raw pointer that is already managed; instead, create one owning smart pointer via std::make_shared / std::make_unique and share ownership only by copying or moving that smart pointer (or using std::dynamic_pointer_cast for polymorphic types).
EXAMPLE: Noncompliant: `int* p = new int; std::shared_ptr<int> p1(p); std::shared_ptr<int> p2(p);`
EXAMPLE: Compliant: `auto p1 = std::make_shared<int>(); std::shared_ptr<int> p2 = p1;`
Avoid storing already-owned raw pointer values in unrelated smart pointers
WHAT: Creating a new smart pointer (e.g., std::shared_ptr) from a raw pointer obtained via get() of another smart pointer causes multiple owners and can lead to double-free and use-after-free.
WHY: Double-free and use-after-free are memory safety violations that can be exploited for code execution, data corruption, or crashes.
HOW: When converting between compatible smart pointer types, always use the appropriate casting utilities (e.g., std::dynamic_pointer_cast, std::static_pointer_cast) so that ownership and reference counts are shared, not duplicated from raw pointers.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): g(std::shared_ptr<D>(dynamic_cast<D*>(poly.get()))); After (safe): g(std::dynamic_pointer_cast<D>(poly));
Avoid unrelated ownership in C++ smart pointers
WHAT: Constructing a new std::shared_ptr from this (or another already-owned raw pointer) that is already managed by a different std::shared_ptr causes multiple owners with independent control blocks, leading to double-free/undefined behavior when either is destroyed.
WHY: Double-free and use-after-free can allow memory corruption, crashes, or code execution.
HOW: Never create a new std::shared_ptr from a raw pointer that is already managed; instead, use std::enable_shared_from_this and shared_from_this() to obtain additional shared_ptr instances tied to the same control block, and ensure there is an existing std::shared_ptr managing the object before calling shared_from_this().
EXAMPLE: Noncompliant: struct S { std::shared_ptr<S> g() { return std::shared_ptr<S>(this); } }; Compliant: struct S : std::enable_shared_from_this<S> { std::shared_ptr<S> g() { return shared_from_this(); } };
Avoid using default operator new for over-aligned C++ types
WHAT: Using the non-placement default operator new to allocate storage for over-aligned types can construct objects at misaligned addresses, causing undefined behavior.
WHY: Misaligned access can lead to crashes, traps in SIMD instructions, or other unpredictable behavior when such objects are accessed.
HOW: For types with stricter-than-fundamental alignment, use aligned allocation APIs (for example, std::aligned_alloc, aligned operator new, or custom allocators) that explicitly honor the required alignment.
EXAMPLE: Before (noncompliant): `auto *p = ::operator new(sizeof(Vector)); new (p) Vector();` After (compliant): `auto *p = ::operator new(sizeof(Vector), std::align_val_t{alignof(Vector)}); new (p) Vector();`
Avoid default operator new for over-aligned C++ types
WHAT: Using the default operator new for over-aligned types (e.g., struct alignas(32)) can return storage that does not satisfy the required alignment, causing undefined behavior when the object is accessed.
WHY: Misaligned access can lead to crashes, data corruption, or exploitable undefined behavior on architectures that require strict alignment.
HOW: For any over-aligned type, provide custom operator new/operator delete (and operator new[]/delete[] if arrays are used) that obtain correctly aligned storage via std::aligned_alloc or another allocator that guarantees the required alignment; ensure deallocation uses the matching free function.
EXAMPLE: Noncompliant: `struct alignas(32) V { ... }; V* p = new V;`
Compliant (C++17+): `static void* operator new(std::size_t n){ if (void* p = std::aligned_alloc(alignof(V), n)) return p; throw std::bad_alloc(); } static void operator delete(void* p){ std::free(p); }`
Do not alternately input and output from a file stream without an intervening positioning call
WHAT: Alternating reads and writes on the same C++ file stream (opened for update) without an intervening flush or positioning call causes undefined behavior when the file is not at end-of-file.
WHY: Undefined behavior can corrupt data, desynchronize file contents and buffers, or cause logic errors that may be exploitable in security-sensitive code paths.
HOW: After output and before subsequent input, call std::fflush() or a file-positioning function (fseek, fsetpos, rewind, or C++ equivalents via seekg/seekp); after input and before subsequent output (when not at EOF), call a file-positioning function (seekg/seekp) to reset the file buffer state.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `fstream f("data", ios::in|ios::out); f << x; f >> y;` After (safe): `fstream f("data", ios::in|ios::out); f << x; f.seekg(0, ios::cur); f >> y;`
Do not alternately input and output from a file stream without an intervening positioning call
WHAT: Alternating writes and reads on the same std::fstream without a positioning call (seekg/seekp) in between causes undefined behavior and may read unintended data.
WHY: Undefined behavior can lead to corrupted data processing, logic bypass, or exposure of stale or sensitive content in security-critical file operations.
HOW: After writing to a std::fstream and before reading from it (or vice versa), always perform an appropriate positioning call (for example, seekg or seekp) to reset the file position and synchronize the stream state.
EXAMPLE: Before (noncompliant, C++): `file << "data"; std::string s; file >> s;` After (compliant): `file << "data"; file.seekg(0, std::ios::beg); std::string s; file >> s;`
Close files when they are no longer needed
WHAT: Failing to call std::basic_filebuf<T>::close() (or to let std::fstream / std::ifstream / std::ofstream destructors run) leaves files open when execution paths (such as std::terminate/std::abort) bypass normal destruction.
WHY: Unclosed files can leak resources, exhaust file descriptors, corrupt data, or leave sensitive data in an inconsistent or exposed state.
HOW: Ensure every successful std::basic_filebuf<T>::open() is matched with close(), or manage file streams by value so their destructors run; for abnormal termination paths (e.g., std::terminate), explicitly close files before terminating.
EXAMPLE: Before (noncompliant): std::fstream f(name); /* use f */ std::terminate();
After (compliant): std::fstream f(name); /* use f */ f.close(); std::terminate();
Close files when no longer needed
WHAT: Failing to close file streams (e.g., before calling std::terminate()) can leave file descriptors and buffers in an undefined or inconsistent state.
WHY: Unclosed files can cause data loss, resource exhaustion, and undefined behavior that may be exploitable or lead to denial of service.
HOW: Explicitly call close() on file streams and check for errors before abnormal termination, or rely on RAII by limiting the scope of file objects so they are destroyed (and closed) before termination.
EXAMPLE: Before (noncompliant): std::fstream file(name); /* use file */ std::terminate(); After (compliant): std::fstream file(name); /* use file */ file.close(); if (file.fail()) { /* handle error */ } std::terminate();
Avoid abrupt program termination in C++ error handling
WHAT: Abrupt termination via std::abort(), std::quick_exit(), std::_Exit(), or implicit/explicit std::terminate() can bypass destructors, atexit handlers, and stream flushing, leaving resources in an indeterminate state.
WHY: Skipped cleanup can corrupt data, leak or lock files, break network protocols, and leave the system in an inconsistent or insecure state after failures.
HOW: Use structured exception handling and RAII to ensure deterministic cleanup; reserve abort/terminate-style calls only for unrecoverable, critical errors and centralize them in well-defined failure paths that log and, where possible, flush/close critical resources first.
EXAMPLE: Before: calling std::abort() directly inside normal error branches; After: throw an exception, handle it in a top-level catch block that performs necessary cleanup and only then, if truly unrecoverable, calls std::terminate() or exits cleanly.
Exception and thread-related abrupt termination in C++
WHAT: Program may abruptly terminate or enter an invalid state when exceptions escape from static/thread storage initialization or destruction, atexit/quick_exit handlers, thread entry functions, or when misusing std::thread and condition variables (e.g., joinable threads destroyed, waits with invalid lock state).
WHY: Abrupt termination or undefined behavior can cause denial of service, data corruption, or inconsistent security checks, especially during startup/shutdown or in multithreaded code.
HOW: Catch and handle all exceptions before they leave static/thread storage initializers, destructors, atexit/quick_exit handlers, and thread entry functions; ensure std::thread objects are joined or detached before destruction or reassignment; always satisfy condition_variable and condition_variable_any lock postconditions before calling wait/wait_for/wait_until.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `std::thread t([]{ risky(); }); /* no join/detach */` — t goes out of scope while joinable. After (safe): `std::thread t([]{ try { risky(); } catch (...) { log_error(); } }); t.join();`
Avoid abrupt termination in C++ error handling
WHAT: Abruptly terminating a C++ program via std::terminate(), std::quick_exit(), std::abort(), or std::_Exit() can prevent stack unwinding and destructor execution, leaving resources unfreed and cleanup handlers unsafe (for example, exit handlers that may throw).
WHY: Missing cleanup and partial stack unwinding can cause resource leaks, inconsistent state, and enable denial-of-service by making the process easy to crash or leave in a bad state.
HOW: Avoid explicit or implicit calls to abrupt termination functions; instead, design code to use normal exception handling and call termination functions that run destructors and cleanup (such as std::exit()), and ensure exit handlers and cleanup code do not throw.
EXAMPLE: Before (noncompliant): std::atexit(f); void f() { throwing_func(); } // may call std::terminate() if throwing_func throws. After (compliant): std::atexit(f); void f() noexcept { try { nonthrowing_cleanup(); } catch (...) { /* log and suppress */ } }
Do not abruptly terminate the program
WHAT: Abruptly terminating a program (e.g., via unhandled exceptions or immediate exit) causes uncontrolled shutdown and skipped cleanup/handlers.
WHY: This can leave resources unfreed, corrupt state, or expose inconsistent/partial outputs that may leak information or break security guarantees.
HOW: Catch and handle all expected exceptions, perform necessary cleanup, and use structured shutdown paths (e.g., registered exit handlers) instead of direct termination.
EXAMPLE (C++): Before: `throwing_func(); // may throw, not caught` → After: `try { throwing_func(); } catch (...) { /* handle and clean up */ }`
Avoid abrupt program termination on errors
WHAT: Abruptly terminating the program (for example, calling std::abort(), std::_Exit(), std::terminate()) on errors without reporting them prevents operators from understanding or responding to critical failures.
WHY: Lack of clear error reporting can hinder incident response, obscure root causes, and reduce system reliability and diagnosability.
HOW: Before any intentional, unrecoverable termination, log or report the nature of the problem to an operator or monitoring system; use dedicated failure paths (for example, a fast_fail function) that always report then terminate. Use assert() only when it reports the failure before aborting.
EXAMPLE (C++):
Before: if (critical_error) std::terminate();
After: if (critical_error) { report("Critical function failure"); std::terminate(); }
Handle all C++ exceptions to avoid abnormal termination
WHAT: Uncaught C++ exceptions cause std::terminate() (and usually std::abort()), which may skip stack unwinding and destructors, leaving external resources in an indeterminate state and abruptly stopping the process.
WHY: Abnormal termination can leak or corrupt resources (files, locks, network connections) and is a common vector for denial-of-service attacks.
HOW: Ensure every exception type that can be thrown is caught by a matching handler; at minimum, wrap main() (or top-level thread entry points) in a catch-all that performs cleanup and then terminates in a controlled way.
EXAMPLE:
Before: int main() { f(); }  // f() may throw, nothing catches it
After:  int main() { try { f(); } catch (...) { cleanup_resources(); return EXIT_FAILURE; } }
Handle uncaught exceptions in thread and program entry points
WHAT: Uncaught C++ exceptions escaping main() or thread entry functions (e.g., std::thread start routines) cause std::terminate() and abrupt program termination.
WHY: Abrupt termination can leak resources, leave data in inconsistent state, and break error-handling or recovery guarantees.
HOW: Wrap main() and all thread entry functions in try/catch blocks that catch all exceptions (catch (...)) and perform controlled shutdown, logging, and cleanup of external resources.
EXAMPLE:
Before (noncompliant): void thread_start(){ throwing_func(); } std::thread t(thread_start);
After (compliant): void thread_start(){ try{ throwing_func(); } catch(...){ /* handle/log */ } } std::thread t(thread_start);
Handle all exceptions in thread entry functions
WHAT: Failing to catch exceptions in thread entry functions can allow exceptions to escape and terminate the program or invoke std::terminate.
WHY: Unhandled exceptions in threads can cause abrupt program termination, resource leaks, and inconsistent state, impacting reliability and availability.
HOW: Wrap the body of each thread entry function in a try/catch block that catches all exceptions (catch (...)) and handles or logs them without rethrowing.
EXAMPLE:
Before: void thread_start() { throwing_func(); }
After: void thread_start() { try { throwing_func(); } catch (...) { /* handle/log and allow thread to exit */ } }
Avoid setjmp()/longjmp() for control flow in C++
WHAT: Using setjmp() and longjmp() to simulate exceptions bypasses C++ automatic object destruction, causing undefined behavior, resource leaks, and potential denial-of-service when non-trivial destructors should run.
WHY: Skipped destructors can leak memory and other resources, corrupt program state, and crash or hang the application under error conditions.
HOW: Do not use setjmp()/longjmp() in C++ code; instead, use C++ exceptions (throw, try, catch) or other structured error-handling mechanisms that respect RAII and run all non-trivial destructors.
EXAMPLE: Before (C-style): `if (setjmp(env)) { cleanup(); } ... longjmp(env, 1);`
After (C++): `try { ... } catch (const std::exception& e) { /* cleanup via destructors */ }`
Avoid setjmp/longjmp for error handling in C++
WHAT: Using setjmp() and longjmp() to unwind the stack skips C++ destructors, leaving local objects (e.g., RAII resources) undisposed and causing undefined behavior.
WHY: Skipped destructors can leak resources, leave invariants broken, and create hard-to-predict states that may be exploitable.
HOW: Use C++ exceptions for nonlocal control flow so destructors run during stack unwinding; refactor setjmp/longjmp-based code to throw and catch exceptions instead.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `if (setjmp(env)==0){ f(); } else { /* recover */ }` where `f()` calls `longjmp(env,1);` and owns local RAII objects. After (safe): `try { f(); } catch (const std::exception& e) { /* recover */ }` where `f()` throws on error and all local objects are destroyed automatically.
Avoid setjmp/longjmp for error handling in C++
WHAT: Using setjmp() and longjmp() for control flow bypasses C++ destructors, so automatic objects (RAII resources) are not cleaned up on error.
WHY: Skipping destructors can leak resources, leave inconsistent state, and cause undefined behavior, which may be exploitable.
HOW: Use C++ exceptions (throw/try/catch) for error handling so that stack unwinding runs all destructors and releases resources safely.
EXAMPLE: Replace code that calls setjmp()/longjmp() around resource-using code with try { /* work */ } catch (...) { /* handle */ } and throw to signal errors instead of longjmp.
Do not reference base classes or members in constructor/destructor function-try-block handlers
WHAT: Referencing any non-static member or base class inside a constructor or destructor function-try-block handler causes undefined behavior because those subobjects are already destroyed when the handler runs.
WHY: Undefined behavior can lead to memory corruption, crashes, or exploitable security vulnerabilities due to use-after-destruction.
HOW: In function-try-block handlers for constructors/destructors, only use local variables or static/global objects; move any needed state into locals before the try, or into separate helper functions that do not access destroyed members.
EXAMPLE: Before (noncompliant, C++): `C() try : str(s) { ... } catch (...) { if (!str.empty()) { ... } }` After (compliant): `C() try : str(s) { ... } catch (...) { handle_error(); }` where `handle_error()` does not access `this`, base classes, or non-static members.
Avoid referencing class members in constructor/destructor function-try-block handlers
WHAT: Accessing base classes or data members inside a constructor or destructor function-try-block handler can cause undefined behavior if those members were not fully constructed or are already destroyed.
WHY: Undefined behavior can lead to crashes, data corruption, or exploitable memory-safety vulnerabilities.
HOW: In function-try-block handlers for constructors/destructors, only use fully-initialized inputs (such as constructor parameters) or local variables; do not read or write class data members or base-class subobjects.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `C() try : str(init()) {} catch (...) { log(str); }` → After (safe): `C(const std::string &s) try : str(s) {} catch (...) { log(s); }`
Catch handlers must be ordered from most derived to least derived
WHAT: Incorrectly ordering C++ catch handlers (placing a base-class handler before a derived-class handler) causes derived exceptions to be caught by the base handler and makes derived handlers unreachable.
WHY: Unreachable handlers can skip specialized recovery, logging, or cleanup logic, leading to incorrect error handling and potentially insecure or unstable behavior.
HOW: For each try block, list catch handlers so that handlers for the most derived exception types appear before handlers for their base classes; avoid generic handlers (e.g., `catch (std::exception&)`, `catch (...)`) before specific ones.

WHAT: Incorrect use of condition variables (e.g., calling wait() outside a while loop, or not re-checking the predicate) can cause indefinite blocking, missed notifications, or threads proceeding when their condition is not actually satisfied.
WHY: Such concurrency bugs can lead to deadlocks, data races, and inconsistent shared state, undermining availability and integrity of multithreaded programs.
HOW: Always guard condition_variable::wait() in a while loop that checks the predicate both before and after wait(); use notify_one() only when any waiting thread may safely proceed and only one needs to wake, otherwise use notify_all().

WHAT: Using a single condition variable with different per-thread predicates can cause liveness failures (deadlock) when a notified thread re-enters wait() and no further notifications occur.
WHY: If the awakened thread is not the one whose predicate becomes true next, all threads can end up waiting indefinitely, exhausting the thread pool and halting progress.
HOW: Use a shared predicate that all waiting threads can safely test, or redesign so that each distinct predicate has its own condition variable or explicit scheduling mechanism; always ensure that any thread that may re-wait cannot be the only one capable of issuing further notifications.

WHY: Stalled or deadlocked threads can cause denial of service, resource exhaustion, and unresponsive systems.

Do not speculatively lock a non-recursive mutex already owned by the calling thread
WHAT: Calling try_lock(), try_lock_for(), try_lock_until(), try_lock_shared_for(), or try_lock_shared_until() on a std::mutex, std::timed_mutex, or std::shared_timed_mutex from a thread that already owns that mutex causes undefined behavior.
WHY: Undefined behavior in synchronization can lead to deadlocks, data races, or corrupted shared state, which attackers may exploit to violate integrity or availability.
HOW: Track mutex ownership per thread and ensure speculative locking APIs are only called on non-recursive mutexes that the calling thread does not already own; use std::recursive_mutex / std::recursive_timed_mutex if recursive locking is required.
EXAMPLE: Before (undefined): `std::mutex m; m.lock(); if (m.try_lock()) { /* ... */ }` After (safe): `std::recursive_mutex m; m.lock(); if (m.try_lock()) { /* ... */ }` or avoid the second lock attempt on the same thread.
Avoid speculative locking of non-recursive mutexes already owned by the same thread
WHAT: Locking a non-recursive mutex (e.g., via try_lock in a loop) from a thread that may already hold that mutex can cause undefined behavior, typically deadlock.
WHY: Deadlocks or undefined behavior in synchronization can freeze critical services, corrupt shared state, or break availability guarantees.
HOW: Ensure a thread never attempts to re-lock a non-recursive mutex it already owns; use recursive_mutex only when true re-entrancy is required, or refactor so locking is done at a single, well-defined layer without nested acquisition of the same mutex.
EXAMPLE (C++): Before: `std::lock_guard<std::mutex> l(m); do_work();` where `do_work()` also calls `while (!m.try_lock()) { ... }`. After: Move all locking into `do_work()` and call it without holding `m`, or pass a flag/guard so `do_work()` only locks when not already under protection.
Avoid speculative locking of non-recursive mutexes already owned by the calling thread
WHAT: Locking a non-recursive mutex that is already owned by the same thread (e.g., via speculative locking in a function it calls) causes deadlock.
WHY: Deadlocks can freeze threads, degrade availability, and corrupt shared state if error paths are not executed.
HOW: Ensure a thread does not re-lock a non-recursive mutex it already owns: remove outer locks before calling code that may lock, or use a recursive mutex only when true reentrancy is required and safe.
EXAMPLE: Before (risk): `void f(){ std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m); g2(); } void g2(){ m.lock(); /*...*/ m.unlock(); }` After (safe): `void f(){ g2(); } void g2(){ std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m); /*...*/ }`
Avoid speculative locking of owned non-recursive mutexes
WHAT: Locking a non-recursive mutex that is already owned by the same thread causes deadlock or undefined behavior.
WHY: Such deadlocks can freeze the program, degrade availability, and create hard-to-diagnose failures in concurrent code.
HOW: Track mutex ownership per thread and ensure each non-recursive mutex is locked at most once before being unlocked; use recursive mutexes only when re-entrancy is required and safe.
EXAMPLE: (C++) Before: `m.lock(); /* ... */ m.lock(); // deadlock` After: `m.lock(); /* ... */ m.unlock(); /* ... */ m.lock();`
Do not use std::rand() for security-sensitive randomness
WHAT: Using std::rand() (or C rand()) to generate IDs, tokens, or other security-sensitive values produces predictable, low-quality pseudorandom numbers (short cycles, modulo bias).
WHY: Predictable random values can let attackers guess IDs, tokens, or keys, leading to impersonation, data exposure, or other security breaches.
HOW: For any security- or integrity-related randomness, use a cryptographically secure PRNG or vetted library (for example, <random> with a strong engine, or platform-specific secure RNG APIs), and avoid modulo operations that introduce bias; if you must restrict a range, use rejection sampling or a library helper that does so safely.
EXAMPLE (C++): // Before: insecure
// std::string id = "ID" + std::to_string(std::rand() % 10000);
// After: use a stronger RNG (illustrative only; choose an engine suitable for your platform and threat model)
// std::random_device rd; std::mt19937 gen(rd()); std::uniform_int_distribution<int> dist(0, 9999);
// std::string id = "ID" + std::to_string(dist(gen));
Avoid std::rand() for security-sensitive pseudorandom numbers
WHAT: Using std::rand() for generating pseudorandom values (e.g., IDs, tokens) produces low-quality, biased, and predictable output.
WHY: Predictable or biased random values can let attackers guess IDs, tokens, or keys, leading to impersonation, data exposure, or privilege escalation.
HOW: Use <random> engines (e.g., std::mt19937 or better) seeded from std::random_device (or another high-entropy source), and apply an appropriate std::uniform_*_distribution to avoid modulo bias.
EXAMPLE: Noncompliant (C++): int x = std::rand() % 10001;  // weak, biased
EXAMPLE: Compliant (C++): std::random_device rd; std::mt19937 eng(rd()); std::uniform_int_distribution<int> dist(0,10000); int x = dist(eng);
Properly seed pseudorandom number generators
WHAT: Using a seedable PRNG without explicitly seeding it, or seeding it with a fixed/attacker-controlled value, causes the same random sequence to be generated across runs.
WHY: Predictable “random” values can let attackers guess keys, tokens, nonces, or protocol values, breaking confidentiality and integrity.
HOW: For any seedable PRNG, always initialize it once with a high-entropy, unpredictable seed (for example, from a secure OS RNG or hardware RNG); never use hardcoded constants, timestamps with low entropy, or user input as seeds. Prefer non-seedable true RNGs or secure OS RNG APIs when available for security-critical randomness.
EXAMPLE: Before (C++): `std::mt19937 eng;` → After: `std::random_device rd; std::mt19937 eng(rd());`
Ensure random number generators are securely and unpredictably seeded
WHAT: Using predictable seeds (for example, current time or other attacker-influenced values) for PRNGs causes the same “random” sequence to be generated and allows an attacker to predict outputs.
WHY: Predictable random values can break security mechanisms that rely on randomness, enabling attacks such as token guessing, key prediction, or bypassing protections.
HOW: Use a cryptographically secure source of entropy (for example, std::random_device or OS-provided CSPRNG APIs) to seed PRNGs, and never derive seeds directly from time or other low-entropy, attacker-controllable values.
EXAMPLE (C++ before): std::time_t t; std::mt19937 engine(std::time(&t));
EXAMPLE (C++ after): std::random_device rd; std::mt19937 engine(rd());

WHAT: Using C++ pseudo-random engines (e.g., std::mt19937) with fixed, predictable, or uninitialized seeds leads to predictable “random” values.
WHY: Predictable random numbers can break security mechanisms that rely on randomness (tokens, keys, nonces), enabling guessing and replay attacks.
HOW: For security-sensitive randomness, seed PRNGs with high-entropy values from std::random_device (or a trusted OS entropy source) and never use hardcoded or time-based seeds.

Before: std::mt19937 engine(12345); // predictable
After:  std::random_device dev; std::mt19937 engine(dev());
MSC51-CPP: Ensure your random number generator is properly seeded
WHAT: Using a predictable seed value (for example, current time) for a random number generator makes its output predictable and unsuitable for security-sensitive use.
WHY: Predictable random values can let attackers guess keys, tokens, or other secrets, leading to authentication bypass or data compromise.

Value-returning functions must return on all paths
WHAT: In C++, any value-returning function that reaches the end (including function-try-blocks) without executing a return statement with a value causes undefined behavior.
WHY: Undefined behavior can lead to unpredictable results, data corruption, or exploitable crashes, especially when uninitialized or stale values are used in security-sensitive logic.
HOW: Ensure every control-flow path in a value-returning function ends with a return statement that provides a value; use compiler warnings (e.g., -Wall, -Wreturn-type) and code reviews to verify all branches, including error and exception paths, return a value.
EXAMPLE (C++ before): int absolute_value(int a){ if(a<0){return -a;} }
EXAMPLE (C++ after):  int absolute_value(int a){ if(a<0){return -a;} return a; }
Value-returning functions must return a value on all exit paths
WHAT: Failing to return a value from all exit paths of a value-returning function (including in function-try-block handlers) causes undefined behavior when those paths are taken.
WHY: Undefined behavior can lead to unpredictable control flow, data corruption, or exploitable conditions such as use of uninitialized or stale data.
HOW: Ensure every code path in a value-returning function, including all catch blocks and conditional branches, ends with a well-defined return statement; avoid falling off the end of such functions (except main()).
EXAMPLE (C++ – noncompliant):
std::size_t f(std::vector<int> &v, std::size_t s) try { v.resize(s); return s; } catch (...) { }
EXAMPLE (C++ – compliant):
std::size_t f(std::vector<int> &v, std::size_t s) try { v.resize(s); return s; } catch (...) { return 0; }
Value-returning functions must return on all reachable paths
WHAT: In C++, any value-returning function must return a value on all reachable control paths; missing returns on a reachable path cause undefined behavior.
WHY: Undefined behavior can lead to unpredictable results, data corruption, or exploitable vulnerabilities due to use of indeterminate values.
HOW: Ensure every reachable branch (if/switch/loop/default) in a value-returning function returns a value; only omit a return on paths that unconditionally call [[noreturn]] functions or always throw exceptions.
EXAMPLE:
Before: int f(E e){ if(e==One)return 1; /* missing return for other values */ }
After: int f(E e){ switch(e){case One:return 1;case Two:return 2;default:unreachable("invalid");} }
Do not return from a function declared [[noreturn]]
WHAT: Using a C++ function declared with [[noreturn]] that can fall through and return on some code paths causes undefined behavior.
WHY: Undefined behavior can lead to crashes, inconsistent control flow, and exploitable vulnerabilities in error-handling or termination logic.
HOW: For any [[noreturn]] function, ensure every possible control path either throws, calls std::exit/_Exit/abort, or calls another [[noreturn]] function; do not allow control to reach the end of the function.
EXAMPLE: Before (noncompliant): `[[noreturn]] void f(int i){ if(i>0) throw; else if(i<0) std::exit(0); }`
After (compliant): `[[noreturn]] void f(int i){ if(i>0) throw; std::exit(0); }`
Signal handlers must be plain old functions with C linkage
WHAT: Using a C++-only function (non-POF) or a function without C linkage (for example, `static` C++ linkage) as a signal handler causes implementation-defined or undefined behavior when a signal is delivered.
WHY: Undefined or implementation-defined behavior in signal handlers can lead to crashes, corrupted state, or security vulnerabilities due to inconsistent runtime behavior across platforms and compilers.
HOW: Declare signal handlers with `extern "C"` linkage and ensure they are plain old functions: use only the C/C++ common subset, avoid exceptions, non-POD objects, and calls to non-POF functions (except plain lock-free atomics).
EXAMPLE: Before (noncompliant, C++ linkage): `static void sig_handler(int sig) { /* ... */ }` and `std::signal(SIGTERM, sig_handler);`
After (compliant, C linkage POF): `extern "C" void sig_handler(int sig) { /* C-only operations, no exceptions */ }` and `std::signal(SIGTERM, sig_handler);`
Signal handlers must be plain C functions without throwing exceptions
WHAT: Using C++ signal handlers that can throw or catch exceptions, or that are not declared with C linkage, leads to implementation-defined and unreliable behavior when signals occur asynchronously.
WHY: Improper signal handling can corrupt stack state, break stack unwinding and tracing, and prevent correct error handling, potentially causing crashes or undefined behavior.
HOW: Declare signal handlers with `extern "C"` linkage, ensure they have a simple `void handler(int)` signature, and avoid calling functions that may throw or handling exceptions inside the handler.
EXAMPLE: Before (noncompliant C++): `extern "C" void sig_handler(int){ try { g(); } catch(...){} }` where `g()` may throw; After (compliant): `extern "C" void sig_handler(int){ /* minimal, non-throwing work */ }`
Signal handlers must be plain old functions and avoid non-async-signal-safe features
WHAT: Calling non-async-signal-safe functions (for example, functions that may throw exceptions like g()) directly from a signal handler is unsafe and noncompliant; the handler must be a plain old function that only uses the limited, signal-safe subset of C/C++ features.
WHY: Using non-async-signal-safe features in signal handlers can cause undefined behavior, data corruption, crashes, or deadlocks because the handler may interrupt code that is not reentrant or signal-safe.
HOW: Restrict signal handlers to setting a volatile sig_atomic_t flag or performing other async-signal-safe operations only; move complex logic (including exception-throwing or handling code) into regular functions that are invoked outside the handler after checking the flag.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `extern "C" void sig_handler(int){ g(); }` where `g()` may throw or use non-signal-safe features. After (safer): `volatile sig_atomic_t flag=0; extern "C" void sig_handler(int){ flag=1; } void poll(){ if(flag){ flag=0; g(); } }`
